content: The relative treatment effects on all remaining variables were evaluated using data from 16 outcomes combined across multiple time points. For studies reporting one of these outcomes at multiple time points, the values at the longest follow-up were used. For binary outcomes such as mortality, AIDS-defining illnesses, viral suppression, loss to follow-up, serious adverse events, and regimen substitutions, a logistic regression model with a logit link function and binomial likelihood was employed. To assess heterogeneity, both fixed-effects and random-effects models were utilized. For continuous outcomes, such as increases in CD4 count, linear regression models with an identity link and normal likelihood were applied. The data were analyzed using an arm-based approach, modeling differences in change from baseline across all treatment comparisons. Comparative efficacy estimates were expressed as mean differences or odds ratios, depending on the outcome. The results for all outcomes were presented in network meta-analysis (NMA) cross-tables as odds ratios (OR) or mean differences (MD). Forest plots were used to describe specific treatment comparisons in the main text, while cross-tables were provided in the appendices for more detailed analysis. The GRADE system was applied to assess the quality of evidence. Direct evidence was evaluated as in pairwise meta-analyses, while indirect evidence was assessed using the shortest indirect pathway with the largest number of trials. Evidence was rated as high quality initially and could be downgraded based on five categories of limitations: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and reporting bias. Combined evidence from NMA was also rated, starting with the score from the direct evidence stage. Evidence could be upgraded if indirect estimates improved precision. The parameters of the models were estimated using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method implemented in the JAGS software package. Initial iterations were discarded as burn-in, and inferences were based on additional iterations using two chains. Convergence of the chains was confirmed using the Gelman-Rubin statistic. A systematic literature review identified nine eligible studies, including older treatments no longer relevant today, such as saquinavir and indinavir. The analysis set included 3,877 patients across 16 treatment arms in seven studies. The DAWNING trial, a pivotal randomized, open-label, multinational phase III trial, evaluated the safety and efficacy of dolutegravir (DTG) plus two NRTIs versus lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) plus two NRTIs in HIV-1-infected adults experiencing virologic failure. At week 24, the Independent Data Monitoring Committee recommended discontinuing the LPV/r arm due to higher rates of virologic failure compared to the DTG arm. The study protocol was amended to switch patients from LPV/r to the DTG arm. At week 24, virologic non-response rates were 12% in the DTG arm and 25% in the LPV/r arm. Virologic response rates (<50 copies/mL) at weeks 24, 36, and 48 were higher in the DTG arm compared to the LPV/r arm. Differences in viral suppression were attributed to viral load differences rather than patient discontinuation. The DAWNING trial provided a new connection in the evidence network between LPV/r + 2 NRTIs and DTG + 2 NRTIs. For viral suppression, evidence comparing DTG to LPV/r + 2 NRTIs was available at 24 and 48 weeks, facilitating indirect comparisons. At 24 weeks, evidence was derived from two trials with five treatment arms enrolling 1,075 patients. At 48 weeks, evidence was derived from six trials with 14 treatment arms enrolling 3,223 patients. No statistically significant differences were observed between LPV/r + RAL and either LPV/r + 2 NRTIs or DRV/r + 2 NRTIs. For mortality, the evidence base included 3,600 patients across six trials with 14 treatment arms. Mortality rates were low across trials, with 143 deaths reported. Due to the small number of events, NMA analyses had limitations, often resulting in wide credible intervals. No statistically significant differences were observed between treatments. For discontinuations, the evidence base included 3,599 patients across 14 treatment arms in six trials. Select comparisons from the fixed-effects NMA were statistically significant, but no other comparisons in the network were significant. For discontinuations due to adverse events, the evidence base included 3,599 patients across 14 treatment arms in six trials. The small number of events limited evidence synthesis, and many comparisons had wide credible intervals. No statistically significant differences were observed across the network. For treatment-related and treatment-emergent serious adverse events, the evidence base included 819 patients across four treatment arms in two trials. Few events were observed, and no statistically significant differences were found between treatments. Evidence on treatment-emergent adverse events was based on 3,600 patients across 14 treatment arms in six trials. No statistically significant differences were observed across the evidence network. The GRADE quality assessments for DTG + 2 NRTIs versus LPV/r + 2 NRTIs indicated high-quality evidence favoring DTG for viral suppression at 24 weeks and moderate-quality evidence at 48 weeks. Moderate-quality evidence suggested no statistical difference in discontinuations but favored DTG for discontinuations due to adverse events, based on low-quality evidence. High-quality evidence favored DTG for the proportion of patients experiencing emergent adverse events. Comparisons of DTG + 2 NRTIs versus DRV/r + 2 NRTIs were based on indirect evidence of low or very low quality. For viral suppression at 48 weeks, DTG was associated with a higher proportion of patients achieving suppression, though this was based on low-quality evidence. No other statistically significant differences were observed.
